plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single pressure-temperature plot headed H2O. The vertical axis reads "Pressure, p (atm)" with ticks at 0.006, 1, and 218, and the horizontal axis reads "Temperature, T (C)" with ticks at 0, 0.01, 100, and 374, the spacing on both visibly nonlinear. Two red curves meet at a filled dot labeled "Triple point" at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degrees, with dashed guide lines running to both axes. From that dot one branch rises almost vertically and leans slightly left, while the other sweeps up and to the right, ending at a second filled dot labeled "Critical point" at 218 atm and 374 degrees; below the triple point a single curve continues toward the lower left. Italic letters mark the regions the curves carve out: s at the left, l in the wedge between the branches, and v at the right. Curved arrows tag the branches "Melting", "Boiling", and "Sublimation", and a dashed pair marks the crossing at 1 atm and 100 degrees. Locating a point against these curves tells the reader which phase water occupies there. The plot lays out the coexistence boundaries, including the leftward-leaning melting line whose negative slope means added pressure can melt ice.

interactions.label: Temperature T (°C)
interactions.teaches: Changing temperature moves the state point horizontally, so the phase can change when the point crosses a coexistence boundary

interactions.label: Pressure p (atm)
interactions.teaches: Changing pressure moves the state point vertically, so solid, liquid, vapor, and supercritical behavior are determined by position relative to the red phase boundaries

interactions.label: Pressure near the melting line at T just below 0°C (atm)
interactions.teaches: Because water's melting line leans left, raising pressure at a temperature close to 0°C can cross from the solid region into the liquid region

demo_steps.title: Locate a state point
demo_steps.narration: The sliders place a black state point on the pressure-temperature diagram. The highlighted region shows that phase is determined by location, not by temperature alone.

demo_steps.title: Heat at ordinary pressure
demo_steps.narration: Along the 1 atm path, water crosses the boiling curve near 100°C. The dashed 1 atm and 100°C guides mark the familiar normal boiling point.

demo_steps.title: Raise pressure near melting
demo_steps.narration: With temperature held just below 0°C, increasing pressure moves the point upward across the left-leaning melting curve. The phase label changes from solid to liquid, showing why pressure can melt ice.

demo_steps.title: Choose a low-pressure heating path
demo_steps.narration: At pressures below the triple point, liquid water is not a stable phase. Heating crosses the sublimation boundary, so solid changes directly to vapor.

demo_steps.title: Pass the critical point
demo_steps.narration: A high-pressure path can go above the critical point instead of crossing a normal boiling boundary. Beyond the critical point, liquid and vapor are no longer separated by a sharp phase boundary.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A phase transition occurs when a path in pressure-temperature space crosses a red coexistence curve; water's unusual left-leaning melting line means added pressure can favor liquid over ice.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as a clean 2D pressure-temperature diagram for water with visibly nonlinear axis spacing. Use red phase-boundary curves, black filled dots for the triple and critical points, gray or black dashed guide lines, and italic region labels s, l, and v. The melting curve should be steep and slightly left-leaning from the triple point, the boiling curve should sweep upward to the critical point, and the sublimation curve should extend down-left from the triple point. Interactive overlays should not obscure the textbook curves: use translucent region highlights, a prominent movable black or blue state point, and colored heating paths with small boundary-crossing labels.

authoredContext:
The figure shows the phase diagram for water. Using the graph, if you know the pressure and temperature, you can determine the phase of water. The solid curves—boundaries between phases—indicate phase transitions, that is, temperatures and pressures at which the phases coexist. For example, the boiling point of water is 100°C at 1.00 atm. As the pressure increases, the boiling temperature rises gradually to 374°C at a pressure of 218 atm. A pressure cooker (or even a covered pot) cooks food faster than an open pot, because the water can exist as a liquid at temperatures greater than 100°C without all boiling away. (As we’ll see in the next section, liquid water conducts heat better than steam or hot air.) The boiling point curve ends at a certain point called the critical point—that is, a critical temperature, above which the liquid and gas phases cannot be distinguished; the substance is called a supercritical fluid. At sufficiently high pressure above the critical point, the gas has the density of a liquid but does not condense. Carbon dioxide, for example, is supercritical at all temperatures above 31.0°C. Critical pressure is the pressure of the critical point.

Similarly, the curve between the solid and liquid regions in the figure gives the melting temperature at various pressures. For example, the melting point is 0°C at 1.00 atm, as expected. Water has the unusual property that ice is less dense than liquid water at the melting point, so at a fixed temperature, you can change the phase from solid (ice) to liquid (water) by increasing the pressure. That is, the melting temperature of ice falls with increased pressure, as the phase diagram shows. For example, when a car is driven over snow, the increased pressure from the tires melts the snowflakes; afterwards, the water refreezes and forms an ice layer.

The phase diagram (pT graph) for water shows solid (s), liquid (l), and vapor (v) phases. At temperatures and pressure above those of the critical point, there is no distinction between liquid and vapor. Note that the axes are nonlinear and the graph is not to scale. This graph is simplified—it omits several exotic phases of ice at higher pressures. The phase diagram of water is unusual because the melting-point curve has a negative slope, showing that you can melt ice by increasing the pressure.

Graph of pressure P in atmosphere versus temperature T in degree Celsius for water. The curve starts with going up and right to a point labeled triple point. This is at 0.006 atm and 0.01 degree C. From here, the curve diverges into two branches. One goes up and left and is almost vertical. The other goes up and right. On the branch going up and right is a point at 1 atm and 100 degrees C. Further up on the same branch is a point labeled critical point. This is at 218 atm and 374 degrees C. The area to the left of the left branch is labeled solid. The area between two branches is labeled liquid. The area to the right of the right branch is labeled vapour. The curve to the lower left of the triple point is labeled sublimation, the branch to the upper left of the triple point is labeled melting, and the branch to the upper right of the triple point is labeled boiling.

discrepancies: The default view adds a large light-blue liquid-region fill, a blue 1 atm heating arrow, a purple pressure-sweep line/dot, and an extra black state point; none of these appear in the source static figure and they substantially change the clean black/red diagram.

The source boiling annotation is a black curved leader from the right margin to the red liquid-vapor curve, but the generated figure adds an extra blue 'boiling' label on the horizontal path and makes the black Boiling label visually detached/confusing.
The triple-point label is not formatted like the source two-line label and sits amid extra overlays, reducing clarity around the triple point.
The phase labels and guide region are cluttered by interactive overlays: the 's' region label is crossed/obscured by the purple sweep and dashed guide, unlike the uncluttered source.
The red coexistence curves are broadly correct, but their proportions are somewhat altered, especially the liquid-vapor curve near the critical point and the near-vertical melting curve placement.
evaluation.notes: The underlying H2O phase-diagram structure is recognizable and the interactions are useful, but the default rendering is visually overloaded with added fills, paths, and state markers that prevent it from serving as a faithful drop-in replacement for the source.
action_items: Make the default step match the source figure: remove or hide the phase-region fill, blue heating path, purple pressure sweep, and movable state point until the user activates an interaction.
Restore the boiling annotation to a single black curved leader and label matching the source, and remove the extra blue 'boiling' label from the default view.
Improve label placement around the triple point and solid region so the labels do not compete with guide lines or interactive overlays.
Tune the red coexistence curves and guide positions to more closely match the source proportions, especially the critical-region curvature.
